title: In-process cache, shared cache or CDN?

rows.label: Where it lives
values: Inside each service instance’s own memory
Separate cache servers on your network (Valkey, Redis, Memcached)
Edge servers near users, in front of your origin

rows.label: Who shares it
values: One process only; ten pods means ten separate caches
Every instance of every service that connects to it
Every user routed to that edge location

rows.label: Cost of a hit
values: A memory lookup: nanoseconds to microseconds, no network
Sub-millisecond on the server, plus a network round trip
A round trip to the nearest edge instead of to your origin

rows.label: What it stores
values: Live objects in your language’s own types
Serialised values under keys
Whole HTTP responses: pages, images, scripts, API replies

rows.label: How entries go stale
values: TTL and size limit per instance
TTL per key (`SET … EX`), or delete the key when the source changes
`Cache-Control` max-age or s-maxage from the origin, or a default TTL (24 hours on CloudFront without a cache policy)

rows.label: Invalidating
values: Hard: each instance must be told, or waits out its TTL
Easy: one place to delete or overwrite the key
A purge or invalidation API; CloudFront recommends versioned file names for frequent updates

rows.label: Capacity
values: Counts against each pod’s memory limit; too big and the pod is OOMKilled
The cluster’s RAM; add nodes or shards to grow
Large and managed by the provider; rarely requested files are evicted

rows.label: After a deploy or restart
values: Empty; every new instance warms up from scratch
Still warm; it runs apart from the app
Still warm; deploys of the origin don’t touch it

rows.label: Examples
values: Caffeine, Guava, lru-cache, functools.lru_cache, .NET IMemoryCache
Valkey, Redis, Memcached; ElastiCache, Memorystore, Azure Managed Redis
CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door, Cloudflare

tip: They stack rather than compete. A typical read path is CDN for public HTTP responses, then an in-process cache for the few hottest objects, then a shared key-value cache that all instances agree on, then the database. Put data in the layer whose staleness you can live with: an in-process copy can be out of date per instance for its whole TTL, a shared cache can be fixed with one delete, and a CDN copy lasts until its max-age or a purge.
